title: Edgecase tailwind: mixed-workload benchmarking digest
content:
Context and purpose:
This is a working digest captured during the week of 2026-12-15. Goal: collect observations from mixed-workload runs that produced a reproducible tail-latency oddity when sequences with alternating short+long prompt patterns hit our production-like shadow fleet. Not an RCA yet — this is a runbook + raw notes bundle for triage and next experiments.

High-level summary:
- Pattern: when ~18% of traffic is long-sequence (>=2k tokens) interleaved with short conversational requests (~40–80 tokens) in a bursty arrival process, we observed 99.9th pct spikes increasing by ~1.5–2.2x vs baseline.
- Spike correlates with KV-cache churn and a brief growth in GPU memory pressure on one pod class (A100-40GB, quantized int8 path).
- Not deterministic: requires short-long alternation + a small amount of simultaneous inferred background batch building (continuous batching window at 15ms).
- Immediate mitigation candidates: tighten batching window for mixed workloads; pin long sequences to dedicated pool; probe KV-cache eviction policy.

Run details (representative run):
- test id: EDGE-2026-12-17-03
- fleet config: 8 pods (A100-40GB), runtime v3.7.1-rc2, quant path: int8-optimized, kernel set: default-2026-11
- client pattern: Poisson arrivals lambda=120 qps overall; long requests 18% (uniform length 2048–3072), short requests 82% (40–120). Short/long interleave ratio controlled via script.
- batching config: continuous batching enabled, max-window-ms=15, max-batch-tokens=3000, allow-concurrent-batches=true
- KV cache: enabled, per-request cold-prefix cache miss ratio ~0.12

Observed metrics (delta vs baseline run with only shorts):
- p50 latency: +4ms (negligible)
- p95 latency: +9ms
- p99 latency: +34ms
- p99.9 latency: +120–240ms (this is the tail that triggered alerts)
- GPU memory transient spikes: +200–600MB on affected pods for ~100–350ms windows
- CPU steal/host overhead: small (<=2%)
- KV-cache eviction rate: 3.6x baseline during spikes

Traces and artifacts:
- sampled traces show sequences where long request processing causes KV-cache to flush older prefixes, next short request has to repopulate cache -> extra decoding setup cost -> increased pre-token latency on short requests.
- trace span ordering indicates our prefetch/kv-attach step is occasionally scheduled behind batch construction for long requests due to scheduler fairness.
- artifact: gitlab MR 918 includes a lightweight probe patch to log kv-cache hit/miss per span for experimental runs.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) KV-cache eviction thrash: long requests touch large KV segments and push out hot prefix entries; short requests immediately miss and pay penalty. Impact amplified when batching window groups long+short in same batch.
2) Batching fairness / scheduling: continuous batching logic currently prioritizes batch fullness over request type; long requests cause larger kernel path setup and stall short-case scheduling.
3) Memory allocator fragmentation: for int8-optimized path we see brief allocation spikes when long sequences expand kv buffers — allocator fragmentation plus GC-like cleanup yields transient pause.
4) Hot pod imbalance: small subset of pods (2/8) are more prone due to kernel selection fallback on certain model shims causing extra memory.

Short experiments we ran (and quick outputs):
- Exp A: disable continuous batching (fall back to naive immediate flush): p99.9 reduced by ~55% but p95 increased slightly for longs. Suggests batching behavior contributes heavily to tail.
- Exp B: set max-window-ms=5: tail reduced ~35% vs baseline; throughput dropped ~4% under same qps.
- Exp C: pin long sequences to dedicated pods (2 pods reserved): tail reduced ~60% and average throughput maintained but added capacity cost.
- Exp D: change kv-cache eviction policy from LRU-ish to size-aware (simple MRU bias): preliminary runs show lower eviction rate but occasional memory pressure; needs more tuning.

Conclusions from quick runs:
- Mixing long and short on the same pool is the dominant risk vector for p99.9 degradation when using aggressive continuous batching + kv-cache enabled.
- Mitigations trade off either latency for longs or capacity efficiency.

Open questions / unknowns to verify:
- Are some model variants more prone? (run matrix across 6 models next week)
- Does quantization level (int8 vs int4) change allocation pattern and tail behavior?
- Is there an invisible scheduling race between kv-attach and batch-construction that only appears when allow-concurrent-batches=true?
- What is the exact contribution of host-level GPU driver memory management (NCCL/driver hiccups) vs our allocator?

Next steps (owners and schedule):
- Jonah: run model-matrix sweep (6 models x 3 quant profiles) with mixed workload harness, collect p99/p99.9 + per-span kv hit rates. Target: 2026-12-21.
- Priya: implement and run a micro-experiment toggling allow-concurrent-batches=false on the same fleet to observe scheduler fairness effects. Target: 2026-12-20.
- Diego: audit allocator logs and instrument additional metric for per-request allocation delta (heap and device). Add minimal allocation histogram probe in MR-919. Target: 2026-12-22.
- Lin: work with infra to temporarily label 2 pods as "long-only" in shadow fleet and run 12h soak to measure throughput impact and cost delta. Target: start 2026-12-19 (overnight).
- Maya (me): collate results and prepare short playbook with recommended mitigations (pinning vs batching changes) for ops meeting on 2026-12-23.

Communication plan / temporary mitigation for production:
- For next 48h, recommend we route customer traffic with >1k token requests to a separate capacity tier (if configured) or enable the "dedicated-long-seqs" routing rule in quick mode. This is a conservative mitigation until we confirm impact of scheduling change.
- Notify CS and SRE teams of potential increased cost if dedicated pods are used; give them estimated delta from our pinned-run (approx +12–18% cost for same qps).

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- We should add a synthetic probe that intentionally alternates short/long to catch this in CI benchmarks — currently CI uses single-mode load (short-only) and will miss mixed-workload regressions.
- Consider an adaptive batching policy aware of incoming sequence length distribution where it lowers window if recent variance grows.
- KV-cache eviction tracing needs to be added to runtime-level debug logs with minimal overhead (sampled 0.1% or sampling on tail occurences).

Appendix: quick commands used during the week:
- run harness: tools/bench/run_mixed.sh --qps 120 --long-pct 18 --continuous true --window-ms 15 --out s3://bench/edge-2026-12-17-03
- trace collector: infra/bin/trace-collect --tag EDGE-2026-12-17-03 --sample 0.2 --out /tmp/traces
- kv probe MR: gitlab.com/redwood/runtime/-/merge_requests/918 (probe enabled via feature flag kv-probe)

If you pick this up: start with Jonah's model sweep output and Priya's scheduler toggle — those two will quickly tell us if the issue is policy (batching) vs data-structure (kv thrash). Keep notes in this doc and mark status to in_review once we have MR traces from Diego.

-- end of digest (Maya)
